stem: A client taking oral clindamycin calls the clinic. Which new symptom is most important for the nurse to recognize as requiring prompt evaluation for a serious medication-related complication?
rationale: Clindamycin carries a boxed warning for Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD). Current DailyMed labeling states that CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis and must be considered in patients who develop diarrhea following antibacterial drug use. Frequent watery diarrhea therefore warrants prompt evaluation. Metallic taste and nausea are reported gastrointestinal effects but do not carry the same boxed-warning significance in this scenario; an isolated mild headache is nonspecific.
educational_objective: Recognize new diarrhea during or after clindamycin therapy as a potential sign of C. difficile-associated diarrhea requiring prompt evaluation.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
source_document_title: CLINDAMYCIN HYDROCHLORIDE capsule — Drug Label Information (Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.)
source_locator: BOXED WARNING — Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; WARNINGS — Clostridioides difficile-Associated Diarrhea; ADVERSE REACTIONS — Gastrointestinal
source_claim_supported: Clindamycin can cause C. difficile-associated diarrhea ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis, and CDAD must be considered when diarrhea occurs after antibacterial therapy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — serious antibiotic adverse effect / C. difficile-associated diarrhea
correction_summary: Removed the family-member padding and the unsupported implication that only severe or persistent diarrhea is clinically important. Reframed the item around the boxed warning and used frequent watery diarrhea as the clinically salient finding. Distractors were chosen from minor/nonspecific symptoms rather than absurd mechanisms.
audit_findings: A is the only option linked to the boxed-warning complication in this scenario. B is a reported non-serious taste effect, C is a nonspecific gastrointestinal complaint, and D is nonspecific. The item does not claim that every episode of diarrhea proves CDAD; it correctly requires prompt evaluation. No second answer, cueing, unsupported timing threshold, or unresolved conflict remains.
